summary: Provides a basic set of Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) packages. Several are updates of packages from RFC 2705, including generic, line, trunk, handset, RTP, DTMF and announcement server packages, and five new ones are added. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3660 lists the packages that MGCP gateways and call agents use to agree on telephone tones, events and signals, such as ringback, busy and confirmation tones and the digits of the keypad. Each package is a table saying what each symbol means, who may request it, how it is signalled and how long it lasts. The document also adds five new packages, including one for reserving network resources for a call.

questions: what is in the mgcp generic media package
subtitle: The catalogue of tone, event and signal packages that MGCP gateways use

tldr.problem: MGCP 1.0 defines the protocol but leaves the vocabulary of tones, events and signals to separate packages, and the packages in the earlier RFC 2705 had inconsistencies that made gateways interoperate badly.
tldr.mechanism: The document gives thirteen packages, each a table of event symbols with their meaning, whether the call agent may request them, how they are signalled and how long they last. Eight are updated versions of the RFC 2705 packages and five are new.
tldr.outcome: The packages were registered with IANA, and the document records that the IETF and ITU-T consider the Megaco work in RFC 3525 to be the standards-based way to meet the same needs.

today: RFC 3660 is an Informational memo published in December 2003 that updates RFC 2705, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it. The IESG note in the document points implementers at RFC 3525, the Megaco work that the IETF and ITU-T consider the standards-based way to meet the same needs.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
The document provides a basic set of Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) packages for use with MGCP 1.0 as defined in RFC 3435. The generic, line, trunk, handset, RTP, DTMF, announcement server and script packages are updates of packages from RFC 2705, with additional explanation and in some cases new versions. Five new packages are defined as well: the signal list, resource reservation, media format, supplementary services and digit map extension packages.

The document carries an IESG note. It describes a non-IETF protocol that was being deployed in a number of products, and it tells implementers that RFC 3525, developed in the IETF Megaco Working Group and the ITU-T SG16, is considered by the IETF and ITU-T to be the standards-based way, with reviewed security considerations, to meet the needs that MGCP was designed to address. The Megaco working group and ITU-T Study Group 16 were developing extensions to that document for functions of the kind addressed here.

Several changes were made to the earlier packages for consistency and interoperability. Some signals were changed from type On-Off to type Time-Out, following the clarification in MGCP 1.0 of what On-Off signals mean. The operation complete and operation failure events were added to packages with Time-Out signals, so that by definition all packages containing Time-Out signals now carry them, and a package that defines them itself may override the defaults, which is allowed only to avoid backwards compatibility problems. New events were added in some cases, which moved the affected packages from unversioned to version 1. Some events have aliases, and a recommendation was made to use the alternatives in future, but for maximum interoperability gateways must still implement every event, signal and other item in a package.
sections.plainLanguage: The document tidies up the shared vocabulary that MGCP gateways and call agents use for tones and events, because the earlier version had small differences that stopped gateways from working together. It also says plainly that the IETF and ITU-T regard the newer Megaco work as the standard way to do this.

sections.title: Signals, Events and Package Tables
sections.content:
The document separates two ideas that the word event covers loosely. A signal is a request from a call agent to a media gateway to apply an event, and an event is a request for the detection of something that happens on the media gateway and is notified to the call agent.

Each package lists its events in a table with five columns. The symbol is the unique name used in the package. The definition is a short description. The R column carries an x when the call agent may request the event, and may also carry an S for an event whose state may be audited, a C when the event can be detected on a connection, and a P when the event is persistent. The S column gives the signal type when the event can be signalled: OO for an On/Off signal, TO for a Time-Out signal, and BR for a Brief signal, with a C added when the signal can be generated on a connection. The duration column gives the default duration of Time-Out signals, and where it is left unspecified the default timeout is infinite unless the description says otherwise. A duration may also be declared variable where the amount of time depends on processing time or on the signalling environment, as with scripts or digit out-pulsing.

The call agent may override the default time-out value of any Time-Out event, except those whose default is variable, with a to signal parameter giving the timeout in milliseconds, for example S: sst/cw(to=20000) for 20 seconds. A supplied value may be rounded to the nearest non-zero value divisible by 1000, that is, to a whole second, unless the individual signal says otherwise. On-Off signals are parameterised with a plus sign to turn the signal on and a minus sign to turn it off, and if the parameter is missing the default is to turn the signal on. Unlike Time-Out signals, On-Off signals do not stop when an event occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: A signal is something the call agent asks the gateway to play or do, and an event is something the gateway notices and reports back. Each package is a table of these, with the kind of signal and how long it lasts written alongside.

sections.title: The Generic Media Package
sections.content:
The generic media package, named G, groups the events and signals that can be observed on several types of endpoint, such as trunk gateway endpoints, access gateway endpoints or residential gateway endpoints. It has twelve entries. Some can be requested by the call agent, such as the fax tone, the modem tone and the operation complete and operation failure events, and some are detected on a connection.

Several of the tones are defined in detail, because the frequencies vary by country. The confirmation tone, also called the positive indication tone in ITU-T E.182, uses the same frequencies and levels as dial tone in North America, 350 and 440 Hertz, but with a cadence of 0.1 second on and 0.1 second off, repeated three times. The ringback tone in North America is a combination of two tones with frequencies of 440 and 480 Hertz and levels of -19 dBm each, giving a combined level of -16 dBm, with a cadence for the audible ring tone of 2 seconds on followed by 4 seconds off.

Playing a tone on a phone that is on-hook is an error, and error code 402, phone on-hook, must be returned when it is attempted. The long duration connection event is detected when a connection has been established for more than a provisioned amount of time, with a default of 1 hour. The ringback signal can be applied directly to an endpoint, or to a connection with the syntax rt@connectionID, and the older rbk(connectionID) form is kept for backwards compatibility, with a recommendation that call agents use the newer form.
sections.plainLanguage: The G package holds the tones that any kind of endpoint might produce: busy, confirmation, ringback, fax and modem tones. The document gives exact frequencies for some of them, because those differ from country to country.

sections.title: New Packages and Excluded Packages
sections.content:
Five packages are new in this document: the signal list package, the resource reservation package, the media format package, the supplementary services package and the digit map extension package.

Two packages from RFC 2705 are not included, the MF and the NAS packages. They remain valid, as do all the unversioned packages defined there. The MF package is left out because it had no defined way to outpulse MF digits, so MF CAS is now provided by other packages in a separate document. The N package was incomplete, and a new NAS package has been developed and provided in a separate document.

The resource reservation and media format packages differ from the others because they contain new LocalConnectionOptions, which the new extension rules in MGCP 1.0 allow. Future packages of that type must use a package prefix in front of local connection options, in the form <package-name>/<Local Connection Option>, to avoid name-space problems. Because these two packages arrived before MGCP 1.0 was updated, that was not done for them, and the resulting new local connection options were registered with IANA instead. For future cases with a package prefix, only the package name needs to be registered.

The digit map extension package defines the extension digit map letter P, for partial match override, which overrides the shortest possible match behaviour for a digit map entry. The letter at the end of an entry instructs the gateway to treat that entry as a match only if the current dial string does not partially match another entry. Support for the package is strongly recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Five packages are new here, and two from the earlier document are left out because they were incomplete or superseded. Two of the new packages add new kinds of connection option, and the document explains why they did not need the naming prefix that future ones must use.

sections.title: Connection Options for Reservations and Formats
sections.content:
The resource reservation package, named RES, gives local connection option support for resource reservations and an event to indicate reservation loss. Four local connection options are used: reservation request, reservation direction, reservation confirmation and resource sharing.

The reservation request option tells the gateway to make a reservation on a connection using RSVP, and the call agent names the reservation profile, either controlled load or guaranteed service. Asking for best effort service is the way to indicate that no reservation is wanted, and it is the default value for the parameter. Whether RSVP is used at all depends on whether the option was included in a connection request. If a modify connection request needs a change in the reservation but does not include the option, the value defaults to the one saved for that connection, while asking explicitly for best effort on a connection that has a reservation tears that reservation down.

The reservation direction option says which way the reservation runs. The gateway starts emitting RSVP PATH messages when the direction is send-only or send-receive, and starts emitting RESV messages when it receives PATH messages if the direction is receive-only or send-receive. If the direction is missing, the previously saved value is used, and failing that the value is deduced from the connection mode.

The reservation confirmation option sets the pre-condition for acknowledging a successful connection request. With none, the default, the gateway acknowledges without waiting for the reservation to complete. With send-only it acknowledges when the PATH message has been sent and the matching RESV received, with receive-only when the reservation confirm has been received, and with send-receive when both have happened. The media format package, named FM, adds a media format parameter local connection option, similar to the fmtp attribute in SDP and applicable to the same media formats, encoded as the keyword fmtp or o-fmtp followed by a colon and a quoted string.
sections.plainLanguage: Two of the new packages let a call agent say more about a call in the connection request. One asks the gateway to reserve network capacity with RSVP, and says in which direction and when to confirm it. The other carries media format settings in the same style as the format parameters in SDP.

sections.title: Registrations and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Thirteen packages have been registered with IANA with their versions: Announcement (A, version 1), DTMF (D, 1), Digit Map Extension (DM1, 0), Media Format (FM, 0), Generic (G, 1), Handset (H, 1), Line (L, 1), RTP (R, 1), Resource Reservation (RES, 0), Script (SCRIPT, 1), Supplementary Tones (SST, 0), Signal List (SL, 0) and Trunk (T, 1). The extension digit map letter P has been registered for the DM1 package. Four local connection options have been registered: the media format option fmtp, and the reservation options r-cnf for reservation confirmation, r-dir for reservation direction and r-sh for resource sharing.

The security section is short. The MGCP packages contained in this document do not require any further security considerations beyond those indicated in the base MGCP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: All the package names and versions in the document have been registered with IANA, along with the digit map letter and the new connection options. The packages themselves add nothing to the security rules of the base protocol.

viz.caption: THE EVENTS AND SIGNALS OF THE GENERIC MEDIA PACKAGE

items.label: Confirm Tone
items.desc: Brief signal. Uses the dial tone frequencies in North America with a cadence of 0.1 second on and off, repeated three times.

items.label: Congestion Tone
items.desc: Time-Out signal with an infinite duration.

items.label: Fax Tone
items.desc: Generated when a fax call is detected by the presence of the V.21 fax preamble.

items.label: Intercept Tone
items.desc: Time-Out signal with an infinite duration. A country specific tone.

items.label: Long Duration Connection
items.desc: Detected when a connection has been established for longer than the provisioned time, one hour by default.

items.label: Modem Tone
items.desc: The V.25 answer tone or the V.8 modified answer tone, which implies a data call.

items.label: Operation Complete
items.desc: The standard definition of operation complete.

items.label: Operation Failure
items.desc: The standard definition of operation failure.

items.label: Pattern Detected
items.desc: On/Off signal, parameterised with a decimal value from 0 to 999. It requires provisioning agreed between the call agent and the gateway.

items.label: Preemption Tone
items.desc: Time-Out signal with an infinite duration. A country specific tone.

items.label: Ringback
items.desc: Time-Out signal of 180 seconds, an alias for rt@connectionID kept for backwards compatibility.

items.label: Ringback Tone
items.desc: Time-Out signal of 180 seconds, detected on a connection.

viz.caption: THE PACKAGES ADDED AND LEFT OUT

items.title: Signal List (SL)
items.text: New. Plays a comma-separated list of signals one after another, each of type BR or TO.

items.title: Resource Reservation (RES)
items.text: New. Adds connection options for RSVP reservations and an event for reservation loss.

items.title: Media Format (FM)
items.text: New. Carries media format parameters in a connection request, like the fmtp attribute in SDP.

items.title: Supplementary Services (SST)
items.text: New. The tones used by supplementary services.

items.title: Digit Map Extension (DM1)
items.text: New. The letter P, which overrides the shortest match rule for a digit map entry.

items.title: MF package
items.text: Left out of this document but still valid. It had no defined way to outpulse MF digits.

items.title: NAS package
items.text: Left out of this document but still valid. A new NAS package has been provided in a separate document.

viz.caption: THE LOCAL CONNECTION OPTIONS OF THE RES PACKAGE

cells: Whether the gateway makes an RSVP reservation, and with which profile: controlled load, guaranteed service, or best effort as the default
Whether the gateway sends RSVP PATH messages, sends RESV messages, or both
When the gateway acknowledges a successful connection request: immediately, after the send direction, after the receive direction, or after both
Whether the reserved capacity may be shared with other traffic
